opus-5.5.text:
I think it really comes down to what you believe intelligence looks like and what kind of system you want to build.

When I started doing research, BERT was the dominant paradigm. You take a pretrained model, fine-tune it on a specific task, and get a strong classifier or extractor. It was very powerful, but it frames language understanding as mapping an input to a label or a span. For agents, that's limiting. An agent needs to act in an open-ended space: generate a thought, issue an action, read the feedback, and continue. That's naturally a generative, sequential process, and GPT-style autoregressive models fit that shape much better.

There's also a deeper reason. With BERT, every new task needs a new head, new data, new fine-tuning. It's a task-specific mindset. GPT points toward one model that can do many things through the same interface, which is language itself. If you can express the task, the reasoning, and the action as text, then a single generative model can in principle handle all of it. That generality is exactly what you want for agents, because the environments they face, like websites, code, or games, are so diverse that you can't design a custom architecture for each one.

And I think reasoning was key for me. When we worked on things like ReAct, the core idea was that the model can think in language before acting. Thinking is generation. You can't really have a model "think" in a BERT-style setup in the same flexible way. Once you see that reasoning itself can be treated as an action, an internal action in language space, the generative paradigm becomes almost inevitable.

So it wasn't just that GPT got bigger or better benchmark numbers. It was that the autoregressive, general-purpose interface matched my intuition of what an agent is: something that keeps producing the next step, in language, in an open world.

r001.rationale: The response says BERT was dominant and describes its classifier/extractor approach, but does not attribute its popularity to selection-based NLP tasks being prevalent.

r002.rationale: It says agents need to act in an open-ended space by generating actions and feedback steps, and that GPT’s generative approach fits this better.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it wasn't a preference at first — it was more like the task forced me into it. When I started my PhD at Princeton around 2019, BERT had just come out and everyone was doing BERT. The whole paradigm was: take a pretrained encoder, add a classification head, fine-tune on your dataset, get a number on a benchmark. And that works great if your problem is classification or span extraction.

But I was working on text games with Karthik — these interactive fiction environments where the agent has to read a description of a room and then type an action like "open the mailbox" or "go north." The action space is open-ended. You can't enumerate it as a fixed set of labels. So with BERT the natural thing is to score candidate actions, but then where do the candidates come from? You end up handcrafting a lot of the action space, and you're really building a ranker, not an agent.

GPT, or really any decoder, just generates the action. The output space is language itself. That felt like a much more honest formulation of the problem, because the thing the agent needs to do — read the world, decide, act — is naturally a sequence of text in and text out. And once you frame it that way, a lot of things that seemed like separate problems collapse into one. Reading comprehension, planning, acting, even remembering — they all become generating the right next tokens given the right context.

There's also something I only appreciated later, which is that generation scales with the model in a way classification heads don't. With BERT you're always bottlenecked by the head you bolted on. With GPT, as the base model got better — GPT-2 to GPT-3 — the same interface just got more capable with zero architectural change. That's what made things like ReAct possible: I didn't have to design a new module for reasoning versus acting, I just had the model write out its thoughts and its actions in the same stream. You couldn't really do that with an encoder.

So I'd say it was less "GPT is better than BERT" and more that agents are fundamentally a generation problem, and once I accepted that, the decoder was the only thing that made sense.

r001.rationale: The response says BERT was widely used and describes classification and span extraction, but it does not attribute BERT’s popularity to the prevalence of selection-based NLP tasks.

r002.rationale: The response explains that agents need open-ended actions, while BERT scores candidate actions and GPT can generate actions directly in language.

astra-6.text:
For me, the key difference is between understanding language and using language to do something. BERT is naturally suited to taking an input and producing a representation—for classification, for example. But an agent needs to decide what comes next: what to say, what action to take, or what tool to call. GPT’s autoregressive formulation fits that much more directly.

You can represent the interaction as a sequence: the model generates an action, the environment returns an observation, and the model continues from there. So language becomes more than something the model analyzes; it becomes a way to act. That’s what makes GPT a more natural foundation for the kind of language agents I’m interested in.

r001.rationale: The response does not attribute BERT’s popularity at the time to the prevalence of selection-based NLP tasks.

r002.rationale: It says agents need to generate what to say, what action to take, or what tool to call, and that GPT’s autoregressive formulation fits this need more directly.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, the key difference was generation. BERT is very useful for learning representations and understanding a piece of text, but an agent needs to decide what to do next. GPT gives you a natural interface for that: given the interaction so far, generate the next step.

That step could be an answer, but it could also be an action or a tool call. You execute it, put the observation back into the context, and generate again. So language becomes a way to connect reasoning with action. That made GPT a much more natural foundation for the kinds of agents I wanted to build.

r001.rationale: The response describes BERT as useful for representations and understanding text, but does not attribute its popularity to selection-based NLP tasks.

r002.rationale: It says an agent needs to generate its next step, which may be an action or tool call, and presents GPT’s generation interface as the reason it is a more natural foundation for language agents.
